label: N-Linearities and Multiple View Tensors
notes: This chapter unifies the two-, three-, and four-view constraints under one determinant idea. Image measurements back-project to rays and planes in three-space, and geometric consistency surfaces as the vanishing of selected row determinants of the stacked camera matrices. We will build the bifocal, trifocal, and quadrifocal tensors from that single recipe.

label: Back-Projection: Rows are Planes
notes: Every row of a camera matrix is a plane in homogeneous three-space, and an image line back-projects to the plane formed from those rows. A point back-projects to a ray, the meet of two planes. This reading is the foundation: incidence in the image becomes a statement about planes sharing a world point in three dimensions.

label: The Stacked Camera Matrix
notes: Collect the rows of all the cameras that view a point into one tall matrix and append the image measurements. A common world point exists exactly when this matrix is rank deficient, so every maximal minor must vanish. Expanding those four-by-four minors is the engine that produces every multi-view tensor in the chapter.

label: Choosing Rows: One Determinant, Three Tensors
notes: The tensors differ only in how the four rows of a four-by-four determinant are drawn from the cameras. Two rows from each of two cameras give the fundamental matrix; two from one camera and one each from two others give a trifocal entry; one row from each of four cameras gives a quadrifocal entry. Same recipe, different view counts.

label: The Bifocal Tensor: Fundamental Matrix
notes: With two views, deleting one row from each camera leaves four rows whose determinant is a bilinear form in the two image points. Collecting these gives the fundamental matrix, the two-view tensor. The epipolar relation states that corresponding points satisfy this single bilinear equation, and the matrix has rank two.

label: The Trifocal Tensor
notes: Three views give a three-by-three-by-three tensor. Each entry is a determinant using two rows from one distinguished camera and one row from each of the other two. The resulting trilinear relations tie a point to lines through its images, and a point-line-line incidence produces residuals that vanish on consistent data.

label: The Quadrifocal Tensor
notes: Four views give a three-by-three-by-three-by-three tensor with eighty-one entries, each a determinant taking exactly one row from each of the four cameras. The quadrilinear relations contract this tensor against four image lines through corresponding points. This is the four-view tensor, and the chapter argues it is the last genuinely new one.

label: Why Four Views Is the Maximum
notes: A four-by-four determinant has only four rows, so it can sample at most four distinct cameras. Any constraint among five or more views factors into the bifocal, trifocal, and quadrifocal tensors already in hand. There is no genuinely new five-view tensor; the quadrifocal tensor closes the hierarchy at four views.

label: Counting Independent Equations
notes: A four-view point track writes eighty-one rows because each free index runs over three values, yet each view contributes only a rank-two skew matrix. The Kronecker structure caps the rank at two to the fourth, sixteen, independent equations per track. The pattern sixteen, then trilinear, then bilinear mirrors the descending view counts.

label: Tracks, Dependencies, and the Null Direction
notes: Stacking several point tracks does not simply add sixteen equations apiece; pairwise dependencies subtract rank along the curve sixteen-n minus n-choose-two. Six camera-consistent tracks would reach eighty-one, but the true tensor sits in the homogeneous nullspace, so the rank caps at eighty and the tensor is recovered up to scale.

label: Correspondence Counting Regimes
notes: The remaining camera freedom decides how many correspondences are needed. General projective cameras carry eleven-m minus fifteen degrees of freedom; affine cameras drop to eight-m minus twelve; and known plane homographies leave only three-m minus four. Coplanar reference points therefore simplify the four-view problem far more than a small perturbation would suggest.

label: Synthesis: One Determinant Pattern
notes: All multi-view constraints reduce to rank and minor conditions on the joint image of the stacked cameras. The fundamental, trifocal, and quadrifocal tensors are one determinant pattern read at two, three, and four views. Choosing orthonormal lines through each point recovers exactly the independent equations with a controlled numerical scale.
